title: Customer research guide: methods, templates & examples
summary: What customer research is, 10 methods with a question-to-method map, examples from ServiceNow and Brex, and a free research plan template.
body_markdown:
## Customer research methods


Now that you know the benefits of research, how do you go about gathering it? Here are ten methods to research your customers, followed by a table that maps common product questions to the method that answers them.


### Surveys


Surveys are used to gather customer responses to specific questions. For example, a[net promoter score (NPS) survey](https://www.greatquestion.com/templates/NPS-survey) measures customer experience. NPS surveys typically ask respondents if they would recommend your services or product to a friend or colleague.


### Customer interviews


[Customer interviews](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/how-to-conduct-customer-interviews) are a form of qualitative research that take place between businesses and past, present or future customers about their challenges, goals or feedback on your product. The goal is to use the feedback to iterate on products and services.[Customer exit interviews](https://www.greatquestion.com/templates/customer-exit-interview) explore why a customer stopped using your product or service.


### Prototype testing


[Prototype testing](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/prototype-testing-guide) involves sharing an early stage prototype or wireframe with your target audience on a device they would use. The purpose is to assess the viability of your product concept. An effective way to do prototype testing is as a video-based study. You can watch your participants use the product live and pair the video recording with product tracking. Watch this[webinar](https://info.greatquestion.co/en/prototype-testing-webinar) to learn more about video-based prototype testing.


### Usability testing


Usability testing is used to uncover any potential issues with the product design. There are two types,[unmoderated](https://www.greatquestion.com/templates/unmoderated-usability-testing) and[moderated usability testing](https://www.greatquestion.com/templates/moderated-usability-testing) . Usability testing involves the participant using the product or service in real-time. For example, a fintech app might ask a group of participants to use the app to see how the payment functions are working.


**Related read:**[The complete guide to UX research methods](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/ux-research-methods-guide)


### Unmoderated testing


In an unmoderated test, participants complete tasks on their own time while their screen and voice are recorded. Nobody runs the session live, so results often come back within a day or two and you can watch where people hesitate, backtrack, or give up. It suits usability checks on live flows, first-click tests, and prototype reviews. You can't ask follow-up questions in the moment, so the task wording has to be clear. See our[unmoderated testing guide](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/unmoderated-testing-guide) .


### Concept testing


Concept testing shows customers an idea before you build it: a description, a sketch, a landing page, or a rough prototype. You ask whether it solves a problem they have, what they would expect it to do, and how it compares with what they use today. It is quick and cheap, which makes it a good filter for roadmap ideas. Stated interest tends to run high, so watch what people do with the concept as well as what they say. Our[concept testing guide](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/concept-testing-guide) covers study design and question sets.


### Card sorting


In a card sort, participants group topics or features into categories that make sense to them. In an open sort they name the categories; in a closed sort they use categories you provide. The results show how customers think about your product's structure, which helps with navigation, menus, and information architecture. Pair it with[tree testing](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/tree-testing-guide) to check whether people can find things in the structure you settle on. See our[card sorting guide](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/card-sorting) .


### Diary studies


A diary study asks participants to log their experiences over days or weeks, usually through short prompts on their phone. It catches what a single interview misses: habits, workarounds, and problems that only show up on the third or tenth use. Diary studies take longer to run and need more participant support, so keep entries short and check in regularly to stop people dropping out. Our[diary study guide](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/diary-study-guide) walks through setup and prompts.


### Behavioral analytics


Product analytics show what customers actually do: which features they use, where they drop out of a funnel, and how usage changes after a release. Event tracking and session recordings answer what happened and how often, at a scale no interview program can match. They rarely tell you why. Use analytics to find where to look, then follow up with interviews or usability tests with the people who got stuck. Start from a specific question so the dashboards stay useful.


### Review mining


Review mining means reading what customers already say about you and your competitors in public: app store reviews, software review sites, Reddit threads, and community forums. It is secondary research, so it costs little and needs no recruiting. Tag reviews by theme to find recurring complaints and the words customers use for their problems, which also helps with messaging. Reviews skew toward very happy and very unhappy customers, so treat them as a source of questions to test. Our guide to[customer feedback analysis](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/customer-feedback-analysis) covers tagging and theming.
